Title: Green Dashboards, Broken Systems: Why Observability Alone Can't Prove Resilience
Abstract: Observability can tell you what your system is doing, but it cannot prove how it will behave when something breaks. Dashboards may stay green while hidden dependencies, degraded services, or unexpected failure modes quietly put users at risk. This talk explores the gap between visibility and resilience, and why teams need to actively test failure scenarios rather than rely on monitoring alone.

Title: Make Agents Observable: Tracing Decisions, Tool Calls and Recovery
Abstract: AI agents can produce a confident final answer while hiding the most important part of the execution: what context they received, which decisions they made, which tools they called, and where the workflow started to drift. This talk presents an observability model for agentic systems that goes beyond application logs and model latency. We will follow a realistic agent execution from request to outcome and instrument the signals that make it explainable and operable: - context and instruction versions; - structured decisions and route selection; - tool calls, inputs, outputs, and validation results; - model, latency, token cost, retries, and failures; - policy checks, blocked actions, and human approvals; - final outcomes, fallbacks, and recovery attempts. Using an AgentsKit example, we will compare a deterministic path with an agentic path and show how a shared execution trace makes their behavior visible without relying on hidden chain-of-thought. We will also discuss privacy-aware telemetry: what to record, what to redact, and how to preserve useful evidence without collecting unnecessary secrets or personal data. The session closes with practical metrics and debugging patterns for production agents: task success rate, tool error rate, retry loops, escalation rate, cost per successful task, and time to diagnose a failed execution. Attendees will leave with a concrete checklist for instrumenting agent workflows and answering the question every production team eventually faces: did the agent fail, did a tool fail, or did we give the system the wrong context in the first place?

Title: You Can't Debug What You Can't See: Observability for AI Agents
Abstract: Traditional APM tells you a request was slow. It won't tell you an agent burned 40k tokens narrating a wrong answer. Observability for AI agents needs new primitives: session traces across multi-step reasoning, tool attribution (which call cost what), and token budgets as first-class signals. This talk covers what we instrument at StackGen — spans that follow an agent through plan/gather/present, per-tool cost and latency, and evidence checks that show whether output was grounded — plus how we debug a bad session after the fact. You'll leave with an observability starter set that goes beyond dashboards into "why did this agent do that."

Title: AI Coded It, AI Shipped It, Who Owns It?
Abstract: It's 03:47. The pager fires and you open your terminal. The code that broke was written by an AI agent, shipped by another AI agent, and never seen by a human. The SRE agent has already failed. It's on you. Are you ready? Coding agents have already changed how software gets built. The next shift is coming for how we run it in production: SRE agents are starting to triage, correlate, and will soon remediate before a human is awake. PagerDuty's own "Code It, Ship It, Own It" mantra is under real pressure, the "Code It" and "Ship It" parts are increasingly automated, but "Own It"? That hasn't gone anywhere. We've faced this kind of transition before. Civil aviation automated huge parts of flying decades ago, and the answer wasn't to remove pilots, it was to mandate simulator time, so pilots stay sharp for the moments autopilot can't handle. On-call engineers need the same: practiced reps in low-stakes scenarios, not hope that expertise survives on its own once agents take the routine work. This talk looks at what "owning" an incident means when you didn't write the code and an agent already tried and failed to fix it, and lays out what observability and incident tooling needs to provide to make that ownership possible, from helping you to train for the big one, to providing you with support when it happens

Title: Beyond Token Counts: Observability for AI Coding-Agent Trajectories
Abstract: AI coding assistants are increasingly long-running software processes: they search repositories, call tools, modify files, run tests, encounter failures, retry, delegate work to subagents, and eventually produce—or fail to produce—a pull request. Yet most organizations still measure them primarily through token consumption, model latency, and adoption. This talk treats coding agents as an observability problem. We’ll model the full engineering trajectory from task to validated outcome: task → context acquisition → tool use → code edits → tests → retries → pull request → review → outcome We’ll look at how OpenTelemetry-style events can reconstruct these trajectories across tools such as Claude Code and Codex, and derive practical signals including context-acquisition time, failed-test iterations, abandoned work, prompt-to-PR latency, and cost per accepted task. Finally, we’ll build a deliberately simple, explainable trajectory grader that distinguishes a clean one-pass implementation from a session that eventually succeeds after repeated iteration—or never actually satisfies its original acceptance criteria. The goal is not another developer-productivity score. It is evidence you can inspect.

Title: Three Hours Debugging Code I Never Wrote
Abstract: An agent wrote a change. It passed review, it passed CI, and then it took a production path down for about three hours. Nothing in the diff was wrong on its own, which is exactly why it got through, and the failure only existed in the combination of the edits. What made it slow was not the code. My dashboards told me what was happening and roughly where, and then stopped being useful, because the question I actually needed answered was why the change had been written that way. I could not ask the author, and none of the reasoning existed anywhere. Commit message, pull request description, ticket: nothing. That is a gap in what we record rather than a gap in what we measure, and I do not think our tooling has caught up with it yet. I have been shipping AI-generated code to production since I was fourteen. This talk is that incident in detail, what my telemetry did and did not give me while I was in it, and the three things I changed afterwards. Keeping a change small enough that reverting it is genuinely one step. Testing that the revert works instead of assuming it does. And moving the check that matters to before an action executes rather than alerting after it has already landed. I will be honest about what each one costs in shipping speed, because none of them are free. Tool-agnostic, no live demo. If your team is starting to let agents write the changes you are on call for, this is the failure mode I wish someone had described to me first.

Title: From Benchmarks to Business Impact: Evaluating Generative AI in Production
Abstract: As generative AI systems transition from experimental pilots to production environments, traditional evaluation methods often limited to static benchmarks fail to reflect real-world performance. This session introduces a practical, data-driven evaluation framework that connects model behavior to observable system performance and business outcomes. We examine key evaluation dimensions such as factual accuracy, grounding, safety, and task completion, using measurable signals like hallucination rates, response relevance, user feedback, and task success metrics. Attendees will learn how combining automated evaluation pipelines with human-in-the-loop validation improves coverage while capturing nuanced insights for complex and open-ended outputs. The session also explores domain-specific evaluation approaches across use cases like customer support, content generation, and decision support systems. We highlight techniques to detect and mitigate hallucinations, bias, and robustness issues under varying inputs, improving consistency and reliability. Finally, we present a continuous evaluation pipeline integrated into the AI lifecycle, emphasizing monitoring, traceability, and governance. By incorporating feedback loops and observable signals, organizations can ensure auditability and responsible AI adoption. By aligning evaluation strategies with real user interactions and business KPIs, this session equips practitioners to move beyond benchmarks toward building trustworthy, scalable, and production-ready generative AI systems.

Title: AI Systems Are Distributed Systems Now
Abstract: Modern AI applications are evolving beyond prompt engineering. Today’s LLM systems are distributed architectures composed of retrieval pipelines, vector databases, tool calls, background workers, and evaluation services. Yet most teams still debug them like simple scripts. This talk explores how to apply distributed systems principles to AI applications. We will examine how tracing, telemetry, and evaluation signals can make LLM pipelines observable and debuggable. By instrumenting prompts, retrieval steps, tool calls, and model outputs as structured traces, teams can finally understand where failures occur. We will also discuss the growing role of automated evaluation pipelines in production AI systems. These systems continuously measure hallucinations, groundedness, and regression in model behavior, providing the reliability layer that modern AI infrastructure needs. Attendees will leave with a clear architecture for building observable AI systems, practical instrumentation strategies, and a deeper understanding of why the future of AI engineering looks much more like distributed systems than prompt engineering.

Title: Beyond Dashboards: Building Observability into Modern Cloud Architectures
Abstract: Modern systems generate enormous amounts of data, but collecting logs and creating dashboards alone does not guarantee visibility into system behavior. As applications become more distributed and cloud-native, teams need better ways to understand failures, performance bottlenecks, and user impact. In this session, I’ll explore how observability can be designed into modern architectures rather than added as an afterthought. We’ll discuss the role of logs, metrics, traces, and telemetry in improving operational insight and system reliability. I’ll also cover practical lessons around monitoring distributed systems, reducing troubleshooting time, and building feedback mechanisms that help teams detect and resolve issues faster. Attendees will gain practical guidance on implementing observability principles and understanding how visibility across systems can improve reliability, debugging, and operational confidence. Whether you are beginning your observability journey or improving an existing environment, this session offers practical takeaways that can be applied immediately.

Title: Observability for Enterprise AI: Reducing NLP Hallucinations with HITL
Abstract: Enterprise AI systems are increasingly used in legal review, compliance validation, privacy operations, and risk assessment workflows, where hallucinated outputs can create significant operational, regulatory, and financial risk. This session shares practical lessons from designing and evaluating a Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) architecture that improves the reliability and observability of enterprise Natural Language Processing (NLP) systems through layered safeguards, retrieval grounding, and measurable validation pipelines. The talk walks through a production-oriented reliability framework that combines guardrails, retrieval augmentation, and post-generation validation. Attendees will see how prompt templates, instruction constraints, and role enforcement help reduce risky model behavior before generation, while hybrid Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) pipelines using BM25 retrieval, dense vector search, reranking, and multi-query orchestration improve factual grounding and contextual precision. The session also demonstrates how citation enforcement, schema validation, self-critique, and multi-step verification create observable checkpoints that help detect and prevent unverifiable outputs before they reach end users. A key focus is making AI systems easier to monitor, evaluate, and improve over time. The presentation outlines how domain experts participate in the scoring loop using structured rubrics that measure factual correctness, contextual relevance, hallucination severity, and tone alignment. Attendees will also learn practical benchmarking approaches for adversarial prompts, ambiguous queries, missing-knowledge scenarios, and long-context reasoning, along with lessons learned from evaluating system behavior across these conditions. The session further examines hallucination reduction strategies using Hybrid Utility Minimum Bayes Risk (HUMBR), an evaluation framework reported to achieve preference rates of 81% over human-crafted ground-truth outputs in comparative testing. Attendees will leave with an implementation blueprint, observability metrics, validation workflows, and an enterprise rollout checklist for building safer, auditable, and production-grade generative AI systems.

Title: Closing the Semantic Gap with Feedback-Driven Ontology Learning
Abstract: Enterprise analytics agents powered by large language models depend on semantic layers that define metrics, dimensions, and relationships to translate natural language into executable queries. However, these ontologies are typically static and curated by small expert groups, creating two persistent challenges. First, a representation gap arises because a small fraction of users generates most feedback, leaving long-tail analytical patterns underrepresented. Second, a staleness gap emerges as evolving business logic outpaces manual updates, leading to incorrect outputs based on outdated definitions. This talk presents a closed-loop, feedback-driven architecture that continuously refines enterprise ontologies using signals from production interactions. The approach treats ontology elements as parameters in a structured optimization space and applies online convex optimization with regret-bounded updates to minimize user correction frequency. Observability signals—such as rejected outputs, inline corrections, and query reformulations—are transformed into loss functions that guide updates while preserving consistency constraints. Evaluation on a simulated enterprise analytics platform with 1,200 users over 90 days (~200 daily queries) shows measurable gains. The system reduces agent error rates by 31% compared to static ontologies, captures 9× more improvement signals than survey-based methods, and corrects 87% of injected ontology deficiencies. Representation equity improves significantly, with the Gini coefficient dropping from 0.72 to 0.31, indicating better coverage of long-tail usage. These results demonstrate how observability-driven feedback loops can transform semantic layers into continuously improving knowledge systems for analytics agents.

Title: Kubernetes Scaling for Savings and Stability:  Beyond HPA and VPA
Abstract: **The Challenge with Standard Autoscaling** Site Reliability Engineers battle the tension between application reliability and resource bloat. Standard Kubernetes autoscalers rely on broad, shallow metrics like average CPU usage, forcing teams to make coarse and wasteful guesses. This leads to some challenges. 1. **Delayed Decisions:** Simple averages mask the true performance profile of complex applications. 2. **HPA/VPA Conflict:** Independent scaling tools collide, issuing contradictory instructions and causing scaling thrash. 3. **Eviction-Based Resizing:** Legacy VPA requires disruptive pod evictions, increasing cold-start latency for stateful or cache-sensitive workloads. **The Multi-Layered Observability Stack** This session explores how to build smarter, proactive scaling with a rich, multi-dimensional observability pipeline. We will show how to capture and use fine-grained signals across four key layers: * **Container Telemetry (cAdvisor):** Capture micro-burst latency, CPU CFS throttling, and memory working sets, which prevents errant scaling based on benign page cache growth. * **Cluster State (Kube-State-Metrics):** Gain crucial context on workload health, pending replicas, and HPA saturation to ensure scaling is necessary and not already in progress. * **Deep Application Signals (eBPF):** Probe the kernel to surface internal application metrics, such as JVM heap allocation rates and Garbage Collection (GC) pressure. This enables preemptive resource adjustments before OOM events even occur. * **Hardware Accelerators (NVIDIA DCGM):** Detect and scale based on GPU bottlenecks, such as SM utilization or memory bandwidth saturation. **From Insight to Action: The Unified Controller** Observability is only as valuable as the actions it enables. We will demonstrate how to build a unified controller that aggregates the telemetry layers into a state machine. By weighting different application signals and validating cluster state, the controller arbitrates between horizontal and vertical scaling, eliminating HPA/VPA conflict. We will show how to feed this multi-dimensional telemetry directly into the Kubernetes **InPlacePodVerticalScaling API**. Attendees will leave with the blueprints for translating deep observability directly into cluster optimization—mutating CPU and memory allocations on the fly without dropped connections or pod restarts.

Title: Health Checks for Systems. What About Your Team?
Abstract: We monitor everything: liveness probes, SLOs, a dashboard for every service. Yet the engineers holding the pager get a single health check: "How are you doing?" And the answer is always "Fine." This talk applies system-level discipline to team health. Taking inspiration from research on the topic, we'll see how the signals your stack already emits can be turned into an early-warning system for overwork. Then we'll go inside large organizations that run this approach in production today: how they caught unsustainable rotations their dashboards missed, what changed for their on-call teams, and the lessons they learned rolling it out. You'll leave with a practical framework to spot overwork before it turns into resignations.

Title: Your App Is Up. Your Business Is Down.
Abstract: Your monitoring is green. Your app returns a healthy 200 for every check you configured. And your customers can't pay you, because Stripe is degraded and your checkout flow silently died twenty minutes ago. This is what most outages actually look like now. The thing that broke isn't the thing you built. It's the payment provider, the identity provider, the CDN, the LLM API you added last quarter. Your app is fine. Your app is also useless. I work on monitoring, and this talk is about the gap between "is my service responding" and "does my service actually work." I'll go through what dependency-driven failure looks like in practice, why the usual response of adding more checks doesn't fix it, and how you find out what your app depends on in the first place, including the fact that most teams genuinely don't know. I'll also make an argument I'm happy to defend: you can't trust a platform to report its own outage. The party with the incentive to under-report is the same party doing the reporting, which is why an outside observer still matters no matter how good your internal telemetry gets. Practical takeaways for anyone who owns an on-call rotation and has ever watched a dashboard stay green through an incident.

Title: The Fifth Golden Signal: Making Accessibility Observable
Abstract: Most engineering teams monitor latency, traffic, errors, and saturation because these metrics directly impact user experience. We build dashboards, configure alerts, and establish SLOs to detect regressions before users notice them. Yet accessibility regressions are often discovered weeks later through audits, bug reports, or frustrated users. Why? Because accessibility is rarely treated as something that can be observed. In this talk, I'll share how I applied cloud-native observability principles to accessibility by transforming automated accessibility scan results into metrics, dashboards, and trend data using open-source tools. Rather than treating accessibility as a periodic compliance exercise, we'll explore how it can become a continuously monitored signal alongside traditional production metrics. If we believe user experience is worth monitoring, then accessibility deserves a place on the dashboard too.

Title: How Kernel Programming Escaped the Kernel
Abstract: eBPF started as a way to make Linux networking faster. Now it's revolutionizing everything from security to observability to performance optimization, and most engineers don't even know it exists. This talk cuts through the hype to show you what eBPF actually is and why it matters for modern engineering. We'll explore how this kernel technology enables impossible things: zero-overhead monitoring, runtime security enforcement, and network optimization that works at line speed. You'll see eBPF in action across different domains, network monitoring, system call tracing and “encrypted traffic debugging”. From Kubernetes networking to serverless performance, eBPF is quietly powering solutions that seemed impossible just a few years ago. You will be introduced to some useful eBPF scripts that will assist you in your daily tasks, will understand where eBPF fits in your stack and how to start tinkering with it today. It will bee fun!

Title: How to build your own green observability pipeline
Abstract: As a developer, staying curious is the most important trait. Next is getting motivated to build your own projects. In this talk, I guide you throughout my journey of setting up a green observability pipeline, built entirely from open source projects. I'll explain to the audience how to start contributing to open source projects, communicate with maintainers, overcome technical hurdles and complete the mission. A technical talk referenced by a blog post and a GitHub repository.

Title: 404: Observability Without Trade-offs Not Found - Until We Built Gigapipe
Abstract: Every SRE team knows the drill. Prometheus for metrics. Loki for logs. Jaeger or Tempo for traces. Pyroscope bolted on last for profiling. Four services, four storage backends, four things to scale, debug, and pay for. And when an incident hits, you're jumping between all of them trying to correlate signals that were never designed to live together.The trade-off is always the same: observe everything and pay an astronomical bill, or cut costs and fly blind precisely when it matters most. We got tired of it. So we built Gigapipe. Gigapipe is an open-source polyglot observability stack that unifies logs, metrics, traces, and profiles on a single backend, using ClickHouse as the database. It natively implements the industry standards like Prometheus, Loki, Jaeger, Tempo, Pyroscope, and OpenTelemetry APIs, just to name a few. Your existing agents, exporters, and Grafana dashboards work on day one, unchanged. In this talk, we'll cover three things: 1. Why we built it: the real pain that made four services feel unsustainable, 2. How it works: the architecture decisions behind native multi-protocol compatibility on a single storage engine, 3. How you can get involved or run it yourself today: Gigapipe is open-source, under AGPLv3 license, runs as a single binary, and is live in production environments. This is a talk for engineers who've felt the weight of their observability stack and wondered if there's a better way. Spoiler: There is! And you can run it tonight.

Title: Automating peak readiness: turning observability signals into workload engineering insights
Abstract: Building a realistic workload model for peak readiness is still surprisingly manual in most organizations. Developers are interviewed to reconstruct user journeys. Traffic dashboards are manually inspected to estimate peak periods. Concurrent users are approximated in spreadsheets. Multiple teams spend days assembling scenario distributions that are often still inaccurate once the load test begins. The problem is not effort. The problem is that the production truth already exists inside the observability platform — but most organizations lack a systematic way to extract and operationalize it. This session presents an observability-driven workload engineering framework that automatically transforms APM telemetry into production-grade workload models within minutes. Using telemetry from APM and analytics platforms such as New Relic, Dynatrace, AppDynamics, and Google Analytics, we demonstrate how to: • Identify true peak traffic periods from historical telemetry, • Derive real scenario distributions from production user journeys, • Calculate concurrency using session-based analysis derived directly from production telemetry, • Automatically assemble repeatable workload models for load testing and peak readiness exercises. The session includes live examples using NRQL and Dynatrace Real User Monitoring, while keeping the framework vendor-neutral and transferable across observability platforms. Rather than using observability only to explain incidents after they happen, this approach turns production telemetry into a proactive engineering instrument for anticipating and engineering for peak demand before it arrives.

Title: Scalable HIL Architecture: Observability-Driven Validation in Software-Defined Vehicles
Abstract: The transition from isolated electronic control units to software-defined vehicle ecosystems has fundamentally altered how embedded systems are designed, integrated, and validated. Modern vehicle platforms operate as tightly coupled, multi-domain environments where functionality emerges from continuous interaction between distributed software services. This shift introduces significant validation challenges driven by cross-domain dependencies, dynamic runtime configurations, over-the-air updates, and continuous software integration. Conventional approaches, built around static test plans and program-specific Hardware-in-the-Loop setups, are no longer sufficient to ensure system reliability or observability at scale. This presentation introduces a scalable, architecture-driven approach that redefines Hardware-in-the-Loop simulation as a core validation infrastructure with observability built in from the ground up. The proposed framework integrates hardware abstraction, real-time simulation, standardized signal governance, embedded diagnostics, and automation orchestration into a unified validation environment. This layered architecture enables synchronized, repeatable system-level validation across multiple vehicle domains with consistent observability throughout the software lifecycle. A key contribution lies in the native integration of diagnostics and automation, enabling deterministic scenario execution, real-time signal observability, and closed-loop validation workflows. This approach eliminates operator-dependent variability, improves signal integrity, and enhances the ability to capture transient system behaviors that are typically missed in legacy frameworks. The modular design supports reuse across platforms and configurations, allowing validation systems to scale without proportional increases in engineering effort. The session will highlight how embedded observability advances validation reliability, accelerates defect detection, and enables sustainable scaling in increasingly complex embedded environments. It also outlines the foundation for future intelligent validation ecosystems, where data-driven insights and adaptive workflows further enhance system verification in software-defined vehicles.
